pages.text: It began on a rainy afternoon when <name> found an old, leather-bound diary near the school library gate. The cover had strange metallic lines that shimmered faintly, and on the first page were three words written in glowing blue ink: “Ask. Observe. Record.”
Curious, <name> scribbled, “Who owns this diary?” The ink shimmered and rearranged itself: “You do, until the truth is found.” He blinked. “Weird…”
Then, as he wrote, “What will happen next?” the diary glowed again — “Principal Sharma will sneeze loudly.” A second later — Achoo! The sound echoed down the hallway.

<name> laughed in disbelief. The diary could predict the future — just a few seconds ahead! For the next few days, <name> and his best friend Aarav tested it — guessing cricket scores, predicting bell rings, even knowing when the canteen samosas would sell out.
But soon, the diary began glitching. The letters shook, merged, and sometimes vanished mid-sentence. One message flickered in strange code: “Source unstable. Return to origin — Sector 9 Lab.”

Sector 9? That was the restricted science zone near the old observatory — rumored to be a government lab. That night, under the glow of streetlights, <name> and Aarav followed the diary’s flickering arrows.

They discovered an underground door behind a rusted telescope dome. The diary pulsed brighter, unlocking the door automatically. Inside were humming machines, holographic screens, and a massive chamber labeled “Project ChronoInk.”
On one screen, a scientist’s old message played: “The Predictive Diary reads micro-fluctuations in probability waves — but it must never be misused. It learns from its user. It trusts its holder.”

Suddenly, the diary started writing on its own: “Decision time. Knowledge or wisdom?” <name> froze. He could use it to predict anything — exams, weather, even the future of people around him. But he remembered what the scientist had said. Knowledge without care could hurt others.

He took a deep breath and wrote: “I choose wisdom.” The diary glowed warmly and sealed itself, turning into an ordinary notebook. A final message appeared before it faded: “The future belongs to those who think before they act.”

The next day, <name> placed the diary safely in the school science lab, labeling it “For research — handle with care.” He smiled at Aarav. “We may not predict the future anymore… but we can still build it — one good choice at a time.” And as they walked out into the bright morning, <name> felt that curiosity was still the best power of all.
